extracted.intended_audience: general readers, antiquaries, and students of church architecture and ecclesiastical history
extracted.subtask_description: Essay-style antiquarian writing describing and interpreting church architecture, fittings, and related customs (doors, porches, foundations, sculpture, ironwork), aimed at informing and entertaining a general but historically curious readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: First impressions — door as element of architectural value
rubrics_metrics.description: That first impressions have no small influence ... in our estimate of the architectural value of a church the door is an element of some importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A shabby or undignified entrance lowers expectations of the interior; conversely a noble porch or doorway raises thoughts and prepares worshippers for something worthy of the building's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach sequence and enclosure (gates, atrium, cloister)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive approaches often included successive gates and doors, an atrium with a covered portico or cloister, and a fountain or cistern at the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the sequence of approach and the functions of each space (washing, separation of classes, burial in atrium) to show how the architecture encoded liturgical and social practice (example: the church at Tyre with 'great porch', atrium, vestibule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of spaces and controlled access (ostiarii and door-keepers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Special order of door-keepers (ostiarii) existed to keep several classes of persons strictly within the portions assigned to them; keys were solemnly delivered to these ostiarii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note institutional arrangements (who guarded which door, liturgical formulae) as part of interpreting a building's use and hierarchy; mention regional differences (west vs east practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Door placement and plan (early English vs later)
rubrics_metrics.description: In earliest English churches the door was placed in the centre of the western wall; later the people's door was commonly on the south side unless cloisters occupied it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record door locations as indicators of period, liturgical practice, and monastic association (e.g., parish vs monastic churches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and form of early doorways (narrowness, monolithic arches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early doorways could be very narrow and tall; some arches were carved from one stone and decorated with cable moulding or zig-zag moulding (Saxon examples like Sowerford-Keynes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call attention to unusual proportions and construction (single-stone arches, short-and-long work) as evidence for dating and typology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norman recessed arches and development of the porch
rubrics_metrics.description: With the Norman style the door-way deeply sunk in the massive wall and protected by three, four, or more concentric arches suggested the more fully developed shelter of the porch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use features like multiple receding arches and massive Norman mouldings to identify Norman-period work and to discuss the porch's evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculptural decoration of porticoes and tympana
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of saints and angels, or complete scenes from scriptural or ecclesiastical story, filled the expanse of the tympanum or the niches of the columns in many decorated porticoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe iconography (subjects, arrangement) and interpret didactic or devotional purpose (examples: Amiens, Strasbourg, Seville, Palma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism of architectural elements (e.g., two-leaved door)
rubrics_metrics.description: About the twelfth century it became customary to divide the main entrance into two by a pillar; the two-leaved door being thus made symbolical of the two natures of Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out symbolic interpretations of form where authors or medieval commentators (Durandus) supply them; relate symbolism to theological teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: National/style contrasts in decorative richness
rubrics_metrics.description: French thirteenth- and fourteenth-century artists were unrivalled in the beauty and wealth of statuary; English work is often less flamboyant but has notable examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare continental exuberance with local traditions; cite exemplary buildings (Amiens, S. Denis vs Peterborough, Gloucester, Ely) to contextualize local craftsmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notable portal examples as typological markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Named west and north doors (Durham, Llandaff, Peterborough, Ely, Higham Ferrers, Gloucester) serve as exemplars of types: decorated Norman, delicate pointed arches, twin doorways with tympana subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use named examples to illustrate points about period, regional variation, and decorative programs; mention specific sculptural programs (e.g., medallions with New Testament scenes at Higham Ferrers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Galilee / deep porch as liturgical space
rubrics_metrics.description: A Galilee is a porch of unusual depth used for public penance during Lent (examples: Ely, Lincoln, Chichester; parish instances: Boxley, Llantwit, Chertsey, S. Woolos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When present, treat a deep western porch as an architectural space with specific ritual uses and a distinct plan and vaulting worthy of separate description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculptural themes and unusual iconography (Dooms, Hell-mouths, Madonna, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Doorways are often surmounted by themes such as the Last Judgment (Doom), enthroned Lord, Madonna and Child, grotesques, vine emblems, Hell-mouths, apocalyptic symbols of the Evangelists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalog subjects and interpret their theological or local significance; note rare or curious motifs (cruciform figures in circles, frescoes over doors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Door materials and traditional construction (oak, iron, long hinges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical old church doors are massive time-stained oak with heavy iron nails and long broad hinges; simpler panelling to ornate examples occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe materials and hardware as evidence of age, repair history, and craft practice; contrast honest simplicity with ornate treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Door decoration techniques (paneling, carving, tracery, beaten iron)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoration ranges from plain paneling to carved panels (Thoresby Door, S. Mary's Bath), tracery-like designs, and beaten iron-work covering large door surfaces (Sempringham Abbey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the technique, motifs, and patterns (e.g., hammered iron forming tree/animals, initials and dates) as indicators of local workshops and periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medieval blacksmith as artist (ironwork design importance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The medieval blacksmith worked at leisure and often produced beaten ironwork as a form of art, with hinges hammered into wide spreading scrolls or covering almost the entire door.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ironwork design quality and craftsmanship; note contrasts between ancient forged decoration and later clumsy repairs as telling of changing standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bronze doors and panel narrative (Florentine Gates of Paradise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bronze doors, especially the Florentine Baptistery doors (Ghiberti's panels), are among the most splendid doors in the world, containing narrative panels and allegorical figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When bronze doors are present, emphasize panel subjects, sculptural quality, and the historical context (competitive commissions, artists' names like Ghiberti and Brunelleschi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knockers as functional signifiers (sanctuary rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many cathedral doors have knockers often indicating that the place claimed the right of sanctuary; types include heads holding rings, lion's heads, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note knockers both as ornamental metalwork and as legal/social indicators (summoning attendants, signalling sanctuary); give typological examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Porch practical and ritual uses (baptism, marriage, courts, burials, notices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Porches have served as places for baptism, marriage ceremonies at the door, thanksgiving after childbirth, burials, ecclesiastical courts, schools, presentation of dower, and posting legal notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail historical uses with citations (e.g., liturgical rubrics, Chaucer, Edwardian prayer-book changes) to show how architecture accommodated social and ritual functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gateways and chapter-house entrances as associated features
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrances to chapter-houses and the gateways to monastic enclosures are often of great interest though not strictly 'church doors' (examples: York chapter-house doorway, Bristol Norman gateway, Durham gateway, Erpingham Gate at Norwich).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat close and conventual gateways as part of the ecclesiastical ensemble; describe their inscriptions, donor associations, and architectural dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief in foundation sacrifices and immurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Early belief held that foundations were often laid with sacrifices — animals or even humans placed under corner-stones — to secure the building's stability; traditions survive as kirk-grim legends and spectral apparitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing foundations, record local traditions, folk tales, and reported finds (skeletons, legends like Bargest or Cauld Lad) as evidence of ritual beliefs surrounding building foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Found skeletons and embedded remains as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Discoveries of skeletons or human remains embedded in walls or foundations (Holsworthy Parish Church, Bremen Bridge Gate, Darrington Church) can indicate deliberate immurement or sacrificial practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report archaeological finds meticulously, describe context (position, mortar covering, relation to wall settlement) and avoid overinterpretation while noting plausibility of ritual immurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of blood or organic additives in mortar (practical and ritual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices such as adding ox-blood or treacle to mortar were both tied to old sacrificial notions and had practical effects in hardening; modern cement has replaced these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention both the ritual explanation and the pragmatic effect; cite historic anecdotes (Ala-ud-din Khilji, alleged Ashantee practice, masons' reports) but qualify claims.
